name: Ascension protocol / routine posts

card.summary: Forum posts in which a member lays out their full regimen, covering skin, gym, diet and supplements, and tracks before and after photos to show how their look changes.
card.note: Some posted protocols include prescription or research compounds; posts are personal plans, not tested programmes.

quick.overview:
An ascension protocol post is a member's written plan for improving their looks, listing everything they intend to do. Typical headings include heightmaxxing, fat loss, supplements, skincare, training and sometimes surgery.

The point is accountability and feedback: members post the plan, ask others to rate or audit it, and often promise before and after photos.
quick.how: A poster states age, height and goals, lists their diet, exercise, skincare and supplement plan, and invites critique. Followers reply with suggestions or criticism. Some posts are simple lifestyle routines such as steps per day and diet; others include hormones, drugs or planned surgeries.
quick.risks: Posts are personal plans, not clinically tested programmes. Some contain prescription and research compounds taken by teenagers, which medical guidance generally advises against without supervision. Replies from other members are often critical.

lead: Ascension protocols and routines are a posting format on looksmax.org in which members list the full set of changes they plan to make to their appearance, often with a promise to post before and after photos.[1][2] In looksmaxxing vocabulary, ascension refers to a noticeable rise in looks, and by extension in status, that results from working on one's appearance.[5] The post is where a member turns that goal into a written plan, so that the community can comment on it and, later, see whether it worked.

The format helps people look better in a practical way: it forces a broad goal such as getting a better face and physique into specific, checkable parts such as a diet, a training split, a skincare routine, a height plan and, for some, procedures. Members then ask others to rate or audit the plan, which gives them a second opinion before they commit, and a photo log afterwards lets them see whether the routine changed anything.[3][4]

Content varies widely. One post, from a self-described 17-year-old, lists a stack of compounds and says it will run for four months and asks readers to rate it.[1] Another, from a 17-year-old at 5'7, covers heightmaxxing, fat loss with a meat and fruit based diet, 10,000 daily steps and supplements.[2] A third asks others to audit a plan that includes surgery, gear and softmaxxing.[3] Replies range from advice to blunt criticism.[2][3] No studies have examined these protocols as a practice.

angle.text: The post is a planning and accountability tool. Whatever improvement occurs comes from the routines listed in it, such as skincare, training and diet. Feedback before starting and photo tracking afterwards let members adjust the plan.

paras: A typical post gives age, height, weight and a list of tactics by category. Titles such as rate my ascension routine, ascension protocol will post before and afters, and requests for others to audit a plan illustrate the format.[1][2][3][4] Some posters call their own post low effort or unfinished and say they will edit it as the plan develops.[1] Others write long structured plans with sections for each goal.[2][3]

The word ascension comes from incel-era forum vocabulary, in which it described moving up in attractiveness and status; in looksmaxxing it is used for the improvement the plan is meant to produce.[5] The posts sit within the wider split between softmaxxing, meaning non-invasive changes such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness, and hardmaxxing, meaning drugs, surgery and other extreme measures; a single protocol often mixes both.[5]

Looksmaxxing took shape in the 2010s on forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, which Wikipedia lists as the PSL forums, and spread to TikTok in the early 2020s.[5] Protocol and routine threads are one of the formats that carried over from forum culture into video: creators now present routines, before and after clips and face ratings as short videos, and news outlets including the BBC, NPR, The Guardian and The New York Times have covered the trend.[5][6]

The Child Mind Institute describes teenagers keeping photo logs of their progress, posting faces and bodies for rating on forums, and following routines of jaw exercises, weight training and skincare they found online; it says boys as young as 13 take part.[6]

One poster lists a regimen of hormones, a fat burner, oral isotretinoin and peptides and says he will run it for four months, deciding on further steps from results.[1] Another outlines a primal-style diet, vitamin D and K2, magnesium and collagen, along with the aim of reaching 5'9.[2] A third plans several surgeries including spine surgery, rhinoplasty and canthoplasty abroad, alongside recovery-focused compounds.[3]

The examples differ in kind. Routine posts built around diet, steps and sunlight resemble ordinary lifestyle plans, while the protocols naming prescription and research compounds or surgeries resemble clinical treatment plans written by non-clinicians. Replies in the threads reflect that difference.

Replies include criticism of effort, such as a user saying the plan was a lot of work to avoid doing something simpler, and technical critique of post-cycle plans.[2][3] The more ambitious posts draw the most scrutiny, and members sometimes answer a plan by listing what they would change before starting.[3]

Clinicians who have commented on the wider trend focus on the feedback loop. A Child Mind Institute counselor said that teens' self-esteem is already fragile during puberty and that harsh feedback in these communities can reinforce a negative self-image and worsen depression, social anxiety and body dysmorphic disorder; he listed more time spent grooming, irritability and sharply increased social media use as warning signs.[6] Wikipedia notes critics who say rating cultures can feed body dysmorphia, along with medical criticism of specific practices and warnings about unregulated peptides and gray-market drugs.[5]

Medical guidance generally advises that prescription hormones and similar compounds be used under clinician supervision, particularly in adolescents, and some protocol posts are written by teenagers who describe taking them without it.[1][5] No studies have followed people through combined protocols of the kind posted.

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing and PSL rating culture develop on forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net.[5]
Looksmaxxing spreads to TikTok, including routine and before and after content.[5]

lore.intro: Ascension protocol posts are a recurring thread type on looksmax.org.[1][2][3] Members use them to share plans, ask for ratings and, in some cases, document results.

claims.claim: A stacked, detailed protocol can raise looks and height in months
claims.believers: Posters describe multi-compound or multi-surgery plans and expect measurable change within a set number of months.[1][3]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested such combined protocols.

claims.claim: Posting a plan and asking for an audit improves the plan
claims.believers: Posters ask high-IQ or experienced members to review plans before they start.[3][4]
claims.experts: No studies have examined forum plan review; the Child Mind Institute reports that harsh feedback in rating communities can worsen self-image in teenagers.[6]

claims.claim: A natural diet plus movement and sunlight can add height and fat loss
claims.believers: One poster combines a meat, organ and fruit diet with 10,000 daily steps, vitamin D and K2 and expects to reach 5'9.[2]
claims.experts: No studies have tested that diet for height gain.

claims.claim: Tracking before and after photos shows what works
claims.believers: Posters promise before and after photos and treat the images as the proof of a protocol.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's coverage of the culture describes before-and-after content as central to it,[5] and the Child Mind Institute describes teens keeping photo logs of their progress.[6]
